title: The Epicurean Paradox
welcome_lead: Walk through the garden of Epicurus and feel the ancient force of the question theists have spent two millennia answering.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the logical problem of evil from Epicurus to Mackie.
final_note: The logical problem may have been dulled, but the existential edge of evil remains.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The paradox is traditionally attributed to Epicurus (341-270 BCE), though it survives mainly through the Christian writer Lactantius (c. 250-325) in De Ira Dei.

The dilemma forces the theist to deny either God's power, His goodness, or the reality of evil.

J.L. Mackie's 1955 paper 'Evil and Omnipotence' formalises the logical problem. The propositions God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists form an inconsistent triad once we add the quasi-logical truths that good opposes evil and there are no limits on omnipotence.

Mackie examines and rejects various theistic responses, including the free will defence in its standard form.

William Rowe's 1979 paper 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' shifts to the evidential problem.

His famous case of a fawn dying slowly in a forest fire illustrates apparently gratuitous suffering. While such suffering does not strictly entail God's non-existence, it provides strong evidence against it.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.

It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
